issues.legal_issue: A deliberate and fundamental suppression of material facts in a criminal investigation can undermine the prosecution case, unlike a merely defective investigation.
material_facts: The police and investigating officers knew that two accused had sustained numerous injuries during the occurrence and had been referred by police for hospital treatment as in-patients, but the investigation did not examine how those injuries occurred.

The officers denied or failed to disclose material circumstances concerning the prior property dispute, the complaint and attempted reconciliation, the accused persons’ injuries, and the circumstances surrounding the first report.
The first report’s authorship and registration circumstances were doubtful, and the investigation and recovery evidence had further inconsistencies.

The Court found that the suppressed matters affected the account of the occurrence and the possible nature of the offence, and that no unimpeachable evidence supplied a reliable alternative basis for conviction.
issues.conclusion: The investigation was not merely defective but involved conscious suppression that undermined the prosecution’s account; the prosecution case could not sustain conviction in the absence of unimpeachable evidence supporting a different conclusion.
issues.legal_principle: An investigating officer must investigate fairly and seek the truth. A defective investigation does not by itself benefit an accused unless it goes to the fundamental root of the prosecution case. Deliberate suppression of material facts that changes or undermines the prosecution narrative may make the case unsustainable unless unimpeachable evidence supports a different charge or conclusion. The Court relied on Kumar v. State, (2018) 7 SCC 536, and referred to Parbhu v. King Emperor, AIR 1944 PC 73, and Anand Ramachandra Chougule v. Sidarai Laxman Chougala, (2019) 8 SCC 50.

predicates.criminal_prosecution: The state investigated and prosecuted an alleged criminal offence.
predicates.deliberate_suppression_of_material_facts: Investigators knowingly withheld or denied facts material to how the occurrence happened or how the accused were involved.
predicates.concealed_facts_fundamentally_change_the: The facts withheld or denied would materially affect the prosecution’s account of the occurrence or the nature of the alleged offence.
predicates.unimpeachable_evidence_supporting_a_reli: The prosecution presented evidence of such reliability that it independently established a sound basis for conviction despite the suppression.
predicates.prosecution_case_cannot_sustain_convicti: The prosecution evidence is insufficient to sustain a conviction.

issues.definition: When a criminal prosecution rests on deliberate suppression that undermines its account and no unimpeachable evidence supplies a reliable alternative, the prosecution case cannot sustain conviction.

issues.legal_issue: A plausible plea of private defence supported by substantial injuries sustained by the accused in the same occurrence must be assessed on the available evidence, and an unexplained failure to investigate those injuries may create reasonable doubt.
material_facts: Two accused had numerous injuries, were referred by police for treatment, and remained admitted as hospital in-patients after the occurrence.
The prosecution witnesses denied or failed to explain the injuries, and the investigating officers did not investigate their cause or the circumstances in which they were sustained.
The accused relied on the injuries, the prior dispute, and the events preceding the occurrence to raise private defence.
The Court found the plea plausible, found no adequate evidence that the accused had exceeded any right of defence, and considered the prosecution evidence unreliable.
issues.conclusion: The accused had raised a plausible private-defence plea and discharged their burden; they were entitled to the benefit of doubt, with no sufficient basis to find that they had exceeded the right of private defence.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 105 of the Evidence Act, 1872, an accused bears the burden of establishing circumstances supporting a defence on a preponderance of probabilities, a burden less onerous than the prosecution’s burden. A defence need not be pleaded in a particular manner and may arise from the evidence. Sections 96–102 of the Indian Penal Code define the right of private defence, including its limits and its duration while apprehension of danger continues. Substantial injuries sustained by an accused in the same occurrence, if unexplained and uninvestigated, may make the prosecution account doubtful; the exception is where injuries are minor or superficial, or reliable evidence otherwise outweighs the omission. The Court relied on Kashiram v. State of M.P., (2002) 1 SCC 71, Lakshmi Singh v. State of Bihar, (1976) 4 SCC 394, Dahyabhai Chhaganbhai Thakkar v. State of Gujarat, AIR 1964 SC 1563, State of Punjab v. Gurbux Singh, 1995 Supp (3) SCC 734, Vijayee Singh v. State of U.P., (1990) 3 SCC 190, and Dev Raj v. State of H.P., 1994 Supp (2) SCC 552.

predicates.criminal_case_with_private_defence: The accused in a criminal case relied on circumstances suggesting that their conduct was defensive.
predicates.accused_sustained_substantial_injuries_i: One or more accused suffered numerous or substantial injuries during the occurrence being prosecuted.
predicates.prosecution_failed_to_explain_or_investi: The prosecution did not adequately account for the accused persons’ injuries, and investigators did not examine how they were sustained.
predicates.defence_is_plausible_on_the_evidence: The evidence makes the accused’s defensive account reasonably probable rather than merely fanciful.
predicates.reliable_evidence_establishes_excessive_: Reliable evidence establishes that the accused continued to use force after the apprehension of danger had ceased.
predicates.accused_entitled_to_benefit_of_doubt_on_: The accused cannot be convicted because the plausible private-defence account leaves reasonable doubt and excessive force is not established.

issues.definition: Where a plausible defensive account is supported by substantial injuries from the same occurrence that the prosecution leaves unexplained and uninvestigated, and reliable evidence does not establish excessive force, the accused is entitled to the benefit of doubt.

issues.legal_issue: Constructive criminal liability for an offence committed by a member of a group requires proof of an unlawful assembly and a common object shared by the accused; mere presence in an assembly is insufficient.
material_facts: The prosecution alleged that a large group participated in the occurrence and sought to attribute offences to accused through group liability.
The evidence involved over-implication and contradictions, and the Court found insufficient reliable material to establish the necessary common object for all accused.
The Court held that the prosecution had to prove the assembly’s requisite size, its unlawful common object, and the commission of an offence by a member, rather than rely on presence alone.
issues.conclusion: Mere presence in an assembly does not establish constructive liability; the prosecution must prove the unlawful assembly and the accused’s shared common object to the required standard.
issues.legal_principle: Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code imposes vicarious liability where an offence is committed by a member of an unlawful assembly in prosecution of its common object, or is one the members knew to be likely in prosecution of that object. The prosecution must prove the requisite assembly, its unlawful common object, and the accused’s membership with the required shared object; mere presence is insufficient. The Court relied on Ranjit Singh v. State of Punjab, (2013) 16 SCC 752, and the authorities discussed there, including Baladin v. State of U.P., AIR 1956 SC 181, Masalti v. State of U.P., AIR 1965 SC 202, and Bajwa v. State of U.P., (1973) 1 SCC 714.

predicates.group_offence_prosecution: The prosecution seeks to hold an accused responsible for an offence committed by another member of a group.
predicates.accused_was_present_in_group: The accused was present among a group at or around the occurrence.
predicates.reliable_evidence_proves_unlawful_assemb: Reliable evidence establishes an assembly of the required size, an unlawful common object, and that the accused shared that object.
predicates.constructive_group_liability_not_establi: The accused cannot be held vicariously responsible for another member’s offence on the basis of group presence alone.

issues.definition: When a prosecution seeks group liability but reliable evidence does not establish an unlawful assembly and the accused’s shared common object, constructive group liability is not established.

issues.legal_issue: Falsehood or discrepancy in a witness’s evidence does not automatically require rejection of the whole testimony, but inseparable material discrepancies that destroy credibility may make the evidence unusable.
material_facts: The prosecution witnesses gave materially conflicting accounts about the occurrence, the pathway and wall, the injuries to the accused, and the circumstances surrounding the first report.
The Court found that the prosecution evidence did not inspire confidence and that its material parts could not reliably be separated into credible and incredible portions.
The Court also found that the evidence as a whole was insufficient to establish the prosecution case.
issues.conclusion: The evidence could not be salvaged by separating reliable portions from unreliable ones because the material discrepancies and suppression affected its credibility as a whole.
issues.legal_principle: The maxim falsus in uno, falsus in omnibus is not a strict rule of Indian criminal law; courts generally sift reliable evidence from unreliable evidence, treating the principle as a rule of caution. Where material discrepancies undermine the witness’s credibility and the evidence cannot be separated without making it unacceptable, the court may reject it. The Court relied on Anand Ramachandra Chougule v. Sidarai Laxman Chougala, (2019) 8 SCC 50, and referred to Sunil Kundu v. State of Jharkhand, (2013) 4 SCC 422.

predicates.criminal_case_relying_on_witness_testimo: The prosecution relies on witness testimony to prove the accused’s guilt.
predicates.material_discrepancies_destroy_witness_c: The witnesses’ important contradictions or falsehoods undermine confidence in their accounts.
predicates.testimony_cannot_be_separated_into_relia: The credible parts of the testimony cannot be distinguished from the unreliable parts without making the evidence unacceptable.
predicates.inseparable_testimony_cannot_support_con: The inseparable testimony cannot provide a reliable basis for conviction.

issues.definition: When material discrepancies destroy witness credibility and the testimony cannot be separated into acceptable and unacceptable parts, that testimony cannot support conviction.

issues.legal_issue: Motive may be less important when reliable eyewitness evidence establishes the offence, but motive cannot be disregarded when it could materially alter the prosecution account, particularly where private defence is raised.
material_facts: The parties had a prior dispute concerning a pathway, including an obstruction, legal proceedings, a complaint, and an attempted reconciliation before the occurrence.
The accused relied on the dispute and the events preceding the occurrence in support of private defence.
The investigators did not adequately investigate the dispute or the preceding events, although those matters could affect the account of who initiated the confrontation.
The Court found that the omission made the prosecution narrative suspect.
issues.conclusion: The prior dispute and related events were material and could not be brushed aside; their deliberate non-investigation strengthened the doubt about the prosecution’s account and the private-defence plea.
issues.legal_principle: Motive may lose significance when adequate and reliable eyewitness evidence proves the occurrence. It becomes material when it could introduce a perceptible change in the prosecution’s version in favour of the accused, especially when private defence is raised; deliberate avoidance of reliable motive evidence may make the prosecution account suspect. The Court stated this principle in its discussion of motive and connected it to the requirements of a fair investigation.

predicates.criminal_case_with_private_defence: The accused in a criminal case relied on circumstances suggesting that their conduct was defensive.
predicates.motive_evidence_could_materially_change_: Evidence about the reason for the parties’ conflict could materially affect who initiated the confrontation or how it unfolded.
predicates.investigators_deliberately_avoided_that_: Investigators consciously failed to examine available evidence about the motive or preceding dispute.
predicates.prosecution_account_becomes_materially_s: The prosecution’s account is materially doubtful because relevant motive evidence was deliberately avoided.

issues.definition: When a defence makes motive evidence material to how an occurrence began and investigators deliberately avoid that evidence, the prosecution account becomes materially suspect.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may intervene in a criminal appeal where factual findings underlying a conviction are not properly considered or are contrary to the evidence on record.
material_facts: The appeals challenged convictions arising from two trials concerning the same occurrence, as well as acquittals in the later trial.
The Court found that material evidence concerning the accused persons’ injuries, the prior dispute, the investigation, and the prosecution witnesses’ contradictions had not been properly considered.
The Court concluded that the findings supporting conviction were contrary to the evidence and that the material deficiencies could not be overcome.
issues.conclusion: The Court could exercise its appellate power to interfere with the convictions because the material facts had not been properly considered and the findings were contrary to the evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution of India, the Supreme Court may intervene where the findings in a criminal case are not properly grounded in the evidence or are contrary to the record; concurrent findings do not prevent intervention in such circumstances. The Court invoked Article 136 in its assessment of the record.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: An appeal before the Supreme Court challenges a criminal conviction.
predicates.material_evidence_not_properly_considere: The courts below failed to give proper consideration to material evidence bearing on guilt or the defence.
predicates.findings_contrary_to_record: The factual findings supporting conviction conflict with the evidence on record.
predicates.supreme_court_intervention_is_warranted: The Supreme Court may interfere with the conviction in the appeal.

issues.definition: In a criminal appeal against conviction, material evidence that was not properly considered and findings contrary to the record warrant Supreme Court intervention.

issues.legal_issue: A criminal conviction cannot stand where the prosecution evidence leaves reasonable doubt after material suppression, unreliable testimony, and a plausible defence are considered together.
material_facts: The prosecution’s account was affected by the deliberate suppression of the accused persons’ injuries and other facts relating to the prior dispute and the occurrence.
The prosecution witnesses’ accounts had material contradictions, and the Court found the evidence did not inspire confidence or permit reliable separation of credible from unreliable parts.
The accused had a plausible private-defence account supported by their injuries, and the Court found no adequate evidence of excessive force.
The Court found no reliable evidence that could support a different conclusion and held that the accused were entitled to the benefit of doubt.
issues.conclusion: The convictions could not stand; the accused were entitled to the benefit of doubt, and the appeals against conviction were allowed.
issues.legal_principle: The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt and must stand on its own evidence, not on weaknesses in the defence. The accused need only raise a plausible defence that creates doubt; the benefit of reasonable doubt follows if the prosecution fails to establish guilt. The Court relied on Anand Ramachandra Chougule v. Sidarai Laxman Chougala, (2019) 8 SCC 50, and Sunil Kundu v. State of Jharkhand, (2013) 4 SCC 422, and applied the principles concerning fair investigation, private defence, and assessment of witness evidence.

predicates.criminal_appeal_against_conviction: An appeal before the Supreme Court challenges a criminal conviction.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_is_materially_unrel: Material suppression, contradictions, or other deficiencies undermine the reliability of the prosecution evidence.
predicates.accused_has_plausible_defence: The evidence supports a reasonably probable account in the accused’s favour.
predicates.prosecution_has_not_proved_guilt_beyond_: The evidence does not establish the accused’s guilt to the required criminal standard.
predicates.conviction_cannot_stand_and_accused_get_: The conviction must be set aside and the accused receive the benefit of doubt.

issues.definition: When unreliable prosecution evidence and a plausible defence leave guilt unproved beyond reasonable doubt in an appeal from conviction, the conviction cannot stand and the accused receive the benefit of doubt.
